newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH-Tiptoe, through the pastoral leases.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH-Tiptoe, through the pastoral leases.

text.p: Prime Minister John Howard said on Monday that there was no separate National Party policy on Wik, the seemingly intractable debate on what to do about the latest extension of native title.
Well, if there isn't now then there certainly has been because the National Party has called openly for extinguishment of native title in the past.
It now says it is still in favour of extinguishment but might be happy with less.
"I'm saying that there is no change in the National Party's position, which is in favour of extinguishment and certainty," National Party Leader Tim Fischer told reporters on Monday.
"And those two components are something that has to be looked at very carefully when you get down to drafting the details."
But the differences between extinguishment and what Howard is expected to produce are largely symbolic.
MY LAND, YOUR LAND, OUR LAND

The underlying problem with the Wik ruling, for those who have always found it a little difficult to come to grips with, is that one person's rights to land have to be at the expense of of someone else.

In the Wik ruling in December the High Court created new rights for Aborigines on land that the government had leased to pastoralists. When the court created new rights, someone else had to lose -- the farmers or miners currently using the land.
Moreover, the court did not say exactly what rights the Aborigines had, which means that the farmers do not know exactly how far their rights have been diminished.
Regardless of the uncertainty, if the government did nothing then the primary producers would be left with less than they had before December. There is no escaping this conclusion.
But if the government ensures the farmers lose nothing, then the Aborigines lose whatever it is that the High Court has given them.
Neither extreme is politically acceptable, so the solution has to be to define and divide rights to the land in such a way that farmers and Aborigines are satisfied as much as possible.
That's what Prime Minister John Howard is working on.
EXTINGUISHMENT
The National Party and the farmers want extinguishment -- an act from the Federal parliament that simply declares there is no native title on pastoral leases, wiping out the court decision.
(Parliaments can override a court's common law decisions, but not constitutional decisions. Subject to the constitution, they create new rights whenever they like.)

But the farmers do not propose that the Aborigines get nothing. After extinguishing the uncertain court-created rights, they propose to create specific rights to this or that, such as a general access right, which the pastoralists would have to put up with.
So this approach says: reduce the existing rights, whatever they are, to zero and then build them up again to something in between.
HOWARD'S APPROACH
Howard says he will not accept extinguishment.
Judging from what he has said publicly and what has been leaked in the media, the Prime Minister would instead seek to define legislatively whatever native title is.
Since there would be no threat to pastoral activities, we assume that the definition would tend to minimise the Aborigines' rights.
Indeed Aboriginal leaders -- who have met Howard and proposed their own division of rights between pastoralists and local Aborigines -- say the Prime Minister's solution would give them very little.

Aborigines' rights can be greatly diminished merely by the procedure specified for making claims. That procedure might give the farmers certainty for their businesses by restricting claims but greatly stifle the ability of Aborigines to use the land.
So extinguishment need not make much difference. Rather than going to zero and then building up again, one can get the same result by starting where you are and minimising.
No wonder then that Fischer's deputy, John Anderson, said on Monday the National Party's requirements could be satisfied without extinguishment.
COMPENSATION
Note that whichever method is used the government must compensate any Aborigines whose rights are diminished.
The constitution demands that the Federal government fairly compensates people for taking away their property, such as a right to land.
